newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolans unite in parliament, fight in bush.
newsitem.headline: Angolans unite in parliament, fight in bush.

text.p: Angola's former civil war foes united in parliament for the first time on Tuesday, but the future of their national unity government was clouded by renewed fighting between their forces in the bush.

Members of the formerly Marxist MPLA government and deputies from the former Western-backed rebel movement, UNITA, sat together for the first time in a joint parliament elected in 1992 but never convened until now.

Seventy UNITA deputies, 126 MPLA legislators and several opposition party members crammed the Palacio dos Congressos in Luanda for their first plenary session to debate problems in the extension of state control to UNITA-held areas.

The fact that the rebels still control most of the Angolan countryside, including its lucrative northern diamond areas, is seen as the real reason behind fighting that has continued since government troops opened an offensive three weeks ago.
The government says Angolan troops are simply mopping up armed units who fought on the losing side in Zaire and have since entered Angola across its northern and eastern borders.

On Sunday, foreign aid workers were pulled out of eastern towns threatened by the fighting, which is certainly linked to the recent civil war in neighbouring Zaire but may also herald a government bid to eradicate UNITA as a force.
Aid agencies in Luanda said they pulled their people out because of mounting security problems, including a incident in which men threatened to set fire to an agency plane.

Although UNITA's complaints have been uncharacteristically muted, the fighting is seen as a threat to Angola's fragile peace process. A 20-year civil war in the former Portuguese colony ended in 1994. But both sides remain armed and wary.
The army advance coincided with the fall last month of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, who backed the UNITA rebels.

His regime was defeated by the forces of Laurent Kabila, actively supported by Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos. Analysts say dos Santos is clearly seizing a chance to take back some rich UNITA territory, or cripple his old foe.
Aid agency officials said a U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) plane took six foreign relief workers from the towns of Luau and Cazomba in easternmost Moxico province on Sunday.
Their plane was held in Luau by about 20 angry men who stuffed grass into the aircraft and threatened to set it alight.
Aid workers pulled out of the UNITA-controlled towns after reports of troop movements at night along Angola's eastern border with the former Zaire, now Congo.

There are 5,000 United Nations peacekeepers in Angola. On Friday the government allowed the U.N. into Lunda Norte province where the offensive began and U.N. officials reported seeing wounded in hospitals in three towns.
The MPLA and UNITA joined in a power-sharing government in April, but their latest effort in a frequently stalled reconciliation process got off to a typically uneasy start.
UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi, who reportedly sent some of his best troops in a vain bid to prop up Mobutu, refused outright to come to the capital and remains ensconced up-country.
Analysts say the former rebel movement is split between hardliners in the countryside who want to hold on to territory and those open to political compromise and reconciliation.
On Tuesday, however, the joint parliament sat in an atmosphere suggesting the civil war had never happened. Debate was cordial and prepared.

Reaction from UNITA to military strikes in diamond-rich Lunda Norte was subdued. UNITA deputy Antonio Urbano Tchassanha raised the issue briefly, accusing the government of attacking UNITA positions in central Huila and Bie provinces.
These incidents occurred far from the borders with Zaire, he alleged, and could have nothing to do with the government's stated reasons for army activity.
